`README.md`:

```md
# ps2-port-engine

A toolchain and runtime for turning PlayStation 2 games into **native PC
ports**: the game's program decompiled into C++ whose behaviour is checked
against the original machine code, then compiled and run on a host that
provides what the PS2 did - the EE kernel, the IOP, sound, the GS drawn with
Vulkan, the VUs, pads, memory cards, the disc - plus what a PC port wants:
higher resolutions, widescreen, frame pacing, settings, mouse, rumble.

It was built on *Burnout 3: Takedown*
([burnout3-pc](https://github.com/danielgomesvieira2000/burnout3-pc), its
first port). The engine itself is game-independent: a game is a directory
with a `game.json`, its own port code and its test runs, in a repository of
its own.

> **No game material here.** This repository holds no game code, assets,
> disc images or BIOS files. A port is made from a disc image its player
> owns; everything taken from it stays on that player's machine.

## How the pieces fit

```
ps2-port-engine/            this repository (MIT)
  ps2decomp/                the library: ELF/ISO readers, R5900 and VU
                            disassemblers, analysis, the interpreter, symbolic
                            derivation, lifting and structuring, verification
  tools/                    the command-line drivers: isotool, analyze, derive,
                            lift, progress, signatures, port, regress,
                            timeline (the frame-pacing profiler), ...
  runtime/                  ps2rt: PS2 instruction semantics the C++ compiles
                            against (verification and the port alike)
  host/                     the native host: memory, dispatch, threads, kernel,
                            IOP, SPU2, GS + GPU bridge, VIF/VU, devices, window
  gpu/                      the Vulkan display and GS renderer
  signatures/               function names shared between games
  docs/                     METHODOLOGY (what "verified" means), ARCHITECTURE,
                            PORTING (every option of a port)
  tests/                    the toolchain's unit tests
  .claude/skills/           ps2-decomp, ps2-port, ps2-release: the workflow
                            and its rules, for Claude Code

<game>-pc/                  a game's repository (e.g. burnout3-pc)
  engine/                   this repository, a git submodule pinned to a tag
  games/<game>/             game.json, port/ (overrides, PC features, test
                            runs), config/, docs/, tests/
```

A game repository is cloned with `git clone --recursive`. The tools are run
from its root (`python engine/tools/port.py --game games/<game>`), and Claude
Code finds the skills in `engine/.claude/skills`.

## Requirements

* Windows 10/11 x64, Python 3.10+ (standard library; Pillow for the art
  scripts), Visual Studio 2022 with C++ (MSVC, its CMake and Ninja)
* For a port: a Vulkan 1.3 GPU, a processor with AVX2
* A disc image you own, for each game: an .iso, or a CD's raw .bin with its
  .cue (Mode 1 or Mode 2 sectors)

## Starting a port of a new game

1. A repository for it, with this one as its engine:
   `git submodule add https://github.com/danielgomesvieira2000/ps2-port-engine engine`
2. The game's directory, from `templates/`:
   `python engine/tools/port.py init <game> --iso "<your disc image>" --title "<Its Title>"`
   writes `games/<game>/` (game.json with the executable read from the
   disc's SYSTEM.CNF, the port's build, an empty overrides.cpp, the player's
   README, a findings stub) and the repository's `.gitignore`, which keeps
   disc material and the game's code out.
3. The pipeline, from the game repository's root:

   ```sh
   python engine/tools/isotool.py extract "<iso>" <EXECUTABLE> -o games/<game>/extracted/
   python engine/tools/analyze.py   --game games/<game>
   python engine/tools/signatures.py --game games/<game> name
   python engine/tools/derive.py    --game games/<game> --emit --csv
   python engine/tools/lift.py      --game games/<game> --structure --emit --csv
   python engine/tools/port.py      --game games/<game>      # build and run natively
   ```

4. The bring-up loop: each run reports why it stopped; what every game needs
   is fixed here, what only this game needs in its own `port/`. See
   [docs/PORTING.md](docs/PORTING.md) and the skills.

What belongs here: what two games have proved they both need, and the
plumbing every port uses (the host's hooks, settings storage, the profiler).
A game's own features - its menus' mouse support, its widescreen anchors,
its packaging - stay in its repository until a second game needs the same;
then the common part moves here, shaped by both.

An engine version is tagged only after every game's recorded runs pass
against it: `python engine/tools/regress_all.py [<other game repositories>]`.
A game repository then moves its `engine/` submodule to the new tag.

## Tests

```sh
python -m unittest discover -s engine/tests       # from a game repository
python -m unittest discover -s tests              # from this repository
```

The host's own tests build with every port (`ps2host_tests`). A change to the
engine is checked against every game's scripted runs
(`engine/tools/regress.py`) before it is tagged: those need the games' discs,
so they run on a developer's machine, not in CI.

## Legal

This repository contains original tooling only - no game code, assets or
binaries, nothing extracted from a disc. Reverse engineering for
interoperability and preservation is protected in many jurisdictions; the
ports made with it redistribute no game assets and need the player's own disc.

MIT licence: [LICENSE](LICENSE).

```

`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`:

```md
# Toolchain architecture

Python 3.10+, standard library only. No third-party packages, so the toolchain
runs anywhere Python does and cannot rot when a dependency changes.

## Why Python for tools, C++ for sources

**Tools in Python.** The analysis passes are iterative and exploratory - you
rerun them constantly while refining heuristics. Fast iteration matters more
than runtime speed, and the whole pipeline over a 4 MB image finishes in about
five seconds.

**Sources in C++17.** The game is C++, and the RenderWare 3.6 layer beneath it
is C. C++ is the only choice that reproduces the original structure honestly,
and it compiles on a modern host for the eventual port. C would force the class
hierarchies to be faked; anything higher-level could not match.

## Module layout

The engine knows nothing about any one game. A game is a directory under `games/`
with a `game.json` (see the repository README), and every tool takes `--game`
(defaulting to the only game present, or `$PS2_GAME`).

```
engine/ps2decomp/
  game.py      a game's game.json: its files, its layout, $gp detection
  layout.py    the memory layout the interpreter and tests use (per game)
  iso9660.py   ISO9660 reader: directory tree, random access, extraction
  elf.py       32-bit little-endian ELF reader
  r5900.py     Emotion Engine disassembler
  vu.py        Vector Unit microcode disassembler
  analysis.py  function discovery and code/data classification
  symbols.py   strings, address cross-references, pointer tables
  naming.py    names from evidence: kernel stubs, diagnostic strings
  signatures.py relocation-masked function signatures, cross-game library
  emu.py       R5900 interpreter, for verification
  symexec.py   symbolic execution of branch-free functions
  paths.py     control flow, frames, memory, inlining, loops
  calls.py     calling convention: live parameters, preserved registers
  testmem.py   memory profiles for test inputs
  structs.py   struct type recovery (type unification over the whole binary)
  typed.py     renders derived code against recovered types
  cppcheck.py  compiles emitted C++ and runs it against the interpreter
  vu0.py       VU0 macro mode (COP2): the arithmetic model, shared with lifted code
  lift.py      lifts machine code to C++, one statement per instruction
  structure.py the lifted statements with structured control flow and named locals
  liftcheck.py compiles lifted C++ and runs it against the interpreter
  difftest.py  differential-test harness

engine/tools/
  isotool.py    disc inspection and extraction
  analyze.py    full static-analysis pipeline
  disasm.py     annotated assembly emitter
  vudis.py      VU microcode disassembler driver
  vuhazards.py  where VU microcode reads Q, P or the flags early, or stalls
  imagemap.py   byte-level accounting of the image
  candidates.py ranks functions by reconstructability
  derive.py     derives, verifies and emits accessor functions
  lift.py       lifts every function, verifies each, emits the verified ones
  refusals.py   why the functions that were not derived were refused
  blockers.py   which instructions keep functions out of the interpreter
  loops.py      loop shapes, for planning loop support
  inspect_function.py  one function through derive, emit, compile and test
  structtypes.py reports on the recovered struct types
  fields.py     measures field-offset consistency (the groundwork for structs.py)
  matchdiff.py  byte-comparison, kept for if the compiler is ever obtained
  signatures.py names functions, exports them to the library, compares binaries
  progress.py   progress accounting

engine/data/ee_syscalls.csv   EE kernel service numbers -> names
engine/signatures/library.json  named signatures from every game so far

engine/runtime/
  include/ps2rt/  types.h and generated.h, which generated code compiles against,
                  and lifted.h, the register context lifted code runs on
  src/eefpu.cpp   reference EE FPU arithmetic (no IEEE infinities or NaNs)
  src/lifted_support.cpp  multiply/divide, MMI lanes, unaligned access for lifted code
  src/vu0.cpp     VU0 macro mode for lifted code, mirroring vu0.py

engine/host/      the PC port's platform layer (engine/docs/PORTING.md): the
                  kernel, threads and interrupts, DMA, VIF, the VUs in micro
                  mode, the software GS, the IOP over SIF, SPU2, input, the
                  window, timers and the clock (--virtual-time), and
                  --gpu-shadow, which checks the GPU renderer against the
                  software GS frame by frame
engine/gpu/       ps2gpu: SDL3 and Vulkan - the window's presentation, and the
                  GS on the GPU (engine/docs/GPU.md), with its own tests
```

Two more tools watch and read what the port runs: `engine/tools/watchdog.py`
alerts when a long job's log goes silent or its memory grows, and
`engine/tools/vuhazards.py` reads a dump of VU instruction memory (written
beside `--frames` pictures) for the pipeline timing the microcode depends on.

Game-specific code lives with its game: for Burnout 3,
`games/burnout3/tools/vdb.py` and `vdbhash.py` read the ValueDB tuning database.

Each layer depends only on the ones above it, and none of them depend on the
CLI drivers.

## `emu.py` - the R5900 interpreter

This is what makes verification possible without the original compiler. It
executes the integer core, common loads and stores, 128-bit `lq`/`sq`, a COP1
single-precision subset, and the MMI operations the string routines need - enough
for 84.8% of discovered functions. `$gp` is seeded with the game's global
pointer (`0x004E8670` in Burnout 3), detected
from the startup code, because a great many functions reach globals through it.

Anything outside the subset raises `UnsupportedInstruction`. That refusal is the
design: an interpreter that quietly approximated an instruction would hand back
confident wrong answers, which is worse than a gap.

Two correctness details that cost real debugging:

* **Branch-likely nullification.** `beql`/`bnel` skip their delay slot when *not*
  taken. Executing it unconditionally corrupted a mask register inside the SIMD
  `strlen` and made it return wrong lengths for every input.
* **Quadword halves.** `lq`/`sq` must preserve the upper 64 bits of a register,
  because Metrowerks spills callee-saved registers with them. Dropping those bits
  corrupts every restore.

## Deriving functions automatically

Reading and reconstructing one function at a time does not scale. Three modules
turn the mechanical cases into a batch process:

```
symexec.py   expression model + straight-line symbolic execution
paths.py     acyclic control flow, the stack frame, memory, call inlining
derive.py    differential verification and C++ emission
```

### `symexec.py` - the expression model

Registers hold *expressions* instead of values. The tree does two jobs: it renders
as C for a human, and it evaluates against concrete inputs so the derivation can be
tested. Both come from the same tree deliberately - a derivation that cannot be
tested is worth very little.

Floats are modelled as 32-bit **patterns**, not as a separate value domain. That
mirrors the hardware: a float register holds 32 bits, and `lwc1`/`swc1`/`mtc1`/
`mfc1` move them without interpreting anything. Interpretation is confined to the
arithmetic nodes, which is what makes bit moves exact.

Two traversal helpers, `children` and `rebuild`, are the basis of every walk over a
tree, and they **raise** on an unrecognised node type. That is not pedantry: the
earlier hand-written versions silently returned nothing for node types added later,
so arguments nested inside `Not`, `Select` and `SignExtend32` became invisible and
the emitter produced functions referencing undeclared parameters.

### `paths.py` - control flow, frames, memory

Most small functions have a conditional. Those are derived exactly by enumerating
every route from entry to a return and recording the branch conditions along each,
so the function becomes an ordered list of guarded results.

* **Loops and underived calls are refused.** A loop's result depends on a trip count
  that is not a function of the arguments, so no finite expression describes it.
* **The stack frame is modelled separately** from real memory, so a prologue's
  register spills and the matching epilogue reloads cancel instead of looking like
  writes a caller could observe.
* **Stores feed an overlay that later loads consult.** Every derived expression
  refers to memory as it stood on entry, so a setter that returns the field it just
  wrote would otherwise be derived against stale contents. Where aliasing cannot be
  ruled out, the function is refused rather than guessed at.
* **Constant conditions are folded.** A flag stored and immediately loaded back
  yields a constant-true branch; exploring both sides anyway manufactures a path
  that can never run, and `select` picks the first path whose conditions hold, so an
  infeasible path could be chosen.
* **Derived callees are inlined**, which is why derivation runs to a fixed point -
  each pass unlocks the callers of what the previous pass proved. Only *verified*
  callees are offered, so one bad derivation cannot propagate upward.

### `derive.py` - verification and emission

Each derivation is differential-tested against the original machine code before any
source is written, and only the ones that agreed are emitted. The emitted C++ is then
compiled (`cppcheck.py`) and run on the same cases, because what is verified is a
tree and what ships is its rendering; a function whose compiled form disagrees is
dropped.

Memory effects are compared, not just return values. Writes are **journalled and
rolled back** rather than restored from a snapshot of a chosen region: these
functions write to globals far outside any such region, and leaving those changes in
place both corrupted later cases and made correct derivations look wrong. Writes
into the callee's own frame are excluded from the comparison, since the frame is
dead on return and the original makes many such writes while a derived expression
makes none.

A function only counts as `verified` when the test actually varied something. A
constant or a fixed-global read ignores its arguments, so eight argument sets
exercise one input eight times; those are recorded a tier lower rather than
inflating the figure.

### Traps worth knowing about

Every one of these produced plausible-looking wrong output, and none were caught by
reading the code:

* **Operator precedence.** A tree evaluates from its structure, so a rendering bug
  leaves the arithmetic right while the printed C means something else:
  `arg1 << 2 + arg0` is `arg1 << (2 + arg0)` in C.
* **A duplicated renderer.** The emitter kept its own copy of the precedence logic
  so it could print `Read*` helpers, and the two drifted. There is now one renderer
  with the Load form as its only hook.
* **Store ordering.** Expressions refer to entry-state memory, so emitting stores
  before the return inverts a read-modify-write.
* **Shift widths.** Word shifts mask the amount to 5 bits and doubleword shifts to
  6. One mask for both turns a shift of 32 into a shift of zero.
* **`lui` sign extension.** The result is sign-extended into the 64-bit register, so
  `lui 0xFFFF` then `dsrl32 32` is `0xFFFFFFFF`, not 0.
* **Float bit moves.** Holding float registers as host doubles canonicalises NaN
  payloads, altering values a copy must preserve.

## Lifting: the complete tier

Derivation enumerates paths and produces readable expressions, so it cannot
finish large functions: half the executable's code is in functions of 96
instructions or more, where it verified under 8%. Lifting is the mechanical
complement. Each instruction becomes one C++ statement over `lifted::Context`
(all GPRs with their upper 64 bits, HI/LO for both pipelines, the FPU registers,
accumulator and condition). Branches become gotos, and a delay slot is emitted
inside its branch's block, or twice when a jump also lands on it. Calls pass the
whole context. The interpreter is the specification, and each handler has a
lifted counterpart that `test_lift.py` checks against it, family by family.

Verification uses the derivation's test plans and memory, but compares more.
After each case the *entire* register state and every byte written must match
the original. Callees run in the interpreter with the context handed over and
back (`Machine.run_to_return`), so each function is checked on its own. Because
the whole state is compared, the lifter also finds interpreter bugs that
`$v0`-plus-memory comparison let through. `pcpyld $v1, $v1, $v0` was one: the
interpreter wrote the low half before reading the source for the high half.

## Calling functions that are not derived

A derived function no longer has to wait for its callees. A call into a function
that has not been derived is kept as a call (`paths.Call`), passing the arguments
the callee reads (`calls.parameters`, integer and float). Its `$v0` becomes a
`CallResult`, and memory after it is a new *epoch*: `Load` carries the epoch it
reads, so a load after the call is a different value from the same load before.

Such a derivation is no longer a set of guarded expressions over entry memory -
a branch after a call depends on what the call did - so its paths are merged into
a decision tree (`PathDerivation.tree`). Verification runs that tree
(`paths.Execution`): stores within an epoch are held until the next call, the
*original* callee runs in the interpreter, and a load from an earlier epoch reads
memory with the journalled writes since then undone. The emitter
(`derive.StatementEmitter`) writes statements in order, capturing into a local any
value a later statement needs that a store or a call could change. Callees that
were not derived are declared; the compiled check links them back to the
interpreter, so the compiled code is tested against original callees too.

Only call-free derivations are inlined. A derived function that calls an
underived one is called by its own callers, by its emitted signature.

A *barrier* (`paths.Barrier`) is an epoch boundary with no call: where a load may
or may not overlap an earlier store, the held stores are applied and the load
reads the new epoch. The walk's epoch lives on its store overlay (`paths.Overlay`)
because a barrier arises deep inside an instruction step. Emitted code needs
nothing for it - its statements already run in order against live memory.

## `structs.py` and `typed.py` - struct types

Types are recovered by unification in the style of Steensgaard's points-to
analysis, with field offsets. A *type node* stands for every value that is
dereferenced: function arguments, return values, and the contents of pointer
fields. Nodes collect the offsets and widths they are accessed at. Evidence that
two values are the same object joins their nodes: an argument passed into a call,
a returned value, a pointer stored into a field. A displaced pointer passed into a
call (`base + 0x1E4`) records an *embedded* type instead.

What keeps this from collapsing into one type:

* **A conflict guard.** Two nodes join only if every offset both use has the same
  set of widths, checked recursively through pointer fields and embedded types.
  Generic routines - memcpy and the like - are refused at the first type they
  disagree with. A subset rule was tried first and let a node that already mixed
  widths absorb everything.
* **Specific links first.** Links are applied in order of how many callers the
  callee has, so generic routines meet established types and are refused rather
  than fusing types before their own evidence arrives.
* **Only arguments the callee reads.** A register that merely still holds a value
  at a call is not an argument. Linking those was half of all links, and joined
  the arguments of unrelated functions.
* **A flow-aware scan.** Register meanings are carried along paths and intersected
  where paths join; loop heads drop whatever the loop overwrites; code after a
  return is unreachable until a branch reaches it.

The guard compares widths, so width agreement is no evidence of quality. The
independent checks (`engine/tools/structtypes.py`) are float-versus-integer use and
signedness at offsets shared by several functions; without the guard both drop
and one type absorbs 1,422 functions.

Global memory is one more node, `globals`, standing for the whole address space. A
register holding a constant address - from `lui`, or the fixed `$gp` - holds
`(globals, address)`, so global variables are fields of that node at absolute
addresses, and a global whose address is passed to a function becomes an embedded
*global object*. For globals the emitter prefers the object form, so an object's
first field does not read as a separate scalar.

The emitter (`typed.py`) renders a typed value as a *view*: a thin object over a
guest address with an accessor per field, a pointer field returning the view of
its target. A load or store becomes a field access only when it matches the field
exactly - offset, width and signedness - so a wrong type can make the source less
tidy but cannot change its meaning, and the compiled check runs it regardless.
Global variables become `g_004876E8()` / `set_g_004876E8(v)` and global objects
constant views such as `g_0049A278_obj.f_8()`.

Arrays are fields with a stride. An address in the linear form base + offset +
stride * index (`typed.linear`, exact through shifts, multiplies and sums) renders
as `arg0.f_10(i)`; a constant offset on a detected run of fields renders as the
element it is, `arg0.set_f_40(3, 0)`. The derived accesses supply the stride
evidence, since the scan cannot follow a variable index.

`derive.reroll` then folds unrolled loops back up: a block of element writes that
repeats with every index advanced by one common step, and nothing else different,
becomes a `for` loop. It works on the emitted statements, which are generated in a
fixed shape, and only ever on writes of constants or already-captured values, so
the order and content of memory writes are unchanged.
Before emitting, the derived functions' own accesses are added to the graph as
evidence: the scan cannot follow a variable index, but an unrolled loop shows
every concrete access it makes, each already verified.

## `r5900.py` - the disassembler

A stock MIPS disassembler mis-decodes a real PS2 binary, because the R5900 is
MIPS III plus Sony/Toshiba extensions. The ones that matter:

* **MMI** (opcode `0x1C`) - 128-bit integer SIMD, with four nested sub-tables
  (MMI0-MMI3) selected by the shift-amount field, plus `PMFHL`/`PMTHL` and the
  parallel shifts. The entry point alone is 31 `padduw` instructions, so getting
  this wrong derails decoding immediately.
* **`LQ`/`SQ`** (opcodes `0x1E`/`0x1F`) - 128-bit load/store.
* **COP2** - on the EE this is the VU0 macro-mode interface, not a conventional
  coprocessor.
* **MIPS III 64-bit arithmetic**, fully implemented on the EE.

`decode(word, addr)` is a pure function, so analysis passes can decode the same
address repeatedly without bookkeeping. Each `Instruction` carries control-flow
flags (branch, call, return, delay slot, likely-branch) that the later passes
run on.

Correctness is covered by 40 unit tests in `engine/tests/test_r5900.py`, hand-assembled
from the instruction-set documentation so the expected values are independent of
the decoder. Writing them caught a real bug: COP1 packs its register fields
differently from the integer unit (`fd` in the shift-amount field, `fs` in `rd`),
which a shared operand formatter had got wrong.

## `analysis.py` - function discovery

The binary has no symbols and no section boundaries, so everything is recovered.
The passes run in order of decreasing confidence, which keeps false positives
down:

1. **Call-target harvesting.** Every `jal` names a function entry directly. The
   compiler only emits `jal` for real call sites, so a `jal` landing inside the
   image is near-proof. 40,430 call sites resolve to 5,677 accepted targets.
2. **Recursive traversal.** From the entry point and every harvested target, walk
   the control-flow graph, following branches and claiming delay slots, stopping
   at returns. This marks bytes *provably* reachable as code, rather than bytes
   that merely happen to decode.
3. **Pointer-table targets.** Virtual calls and callbacks emit no `jal` at all, so
   their targets are invisible to step 1. Every aligned word pointing inside the
   image is considered, then filtered hard: the target must land on a stack
   prologue or just past another function's terminator, decode as a run of real
   instructions, and **end in `jr $ra`**. That last test is what separates code
   from data which merely decodes - a virtual method has to return. 2,597 accepted,
   37 rejected for never returning.
4. **Prologue scanning.** A final `addiu $sp, $sp, -N` sweep catches the remainder:
   888 more.
5. **Extent from contiguous code.** A function's end is the unbroken run of its own
   instructions from its entry, bridging only short all-nop alignment padding.
   Taking the furthest address *reached* instead lets one tail jump swallow
   everything in between - which it did, until it was fixed.

Each function records *why* it was classified, so results stay auditable rather
than being an opaque guess.

Current result: **9,163 functions**, 86.2% of the image proven to be MIPS code,
99.67% of functions ending in a return, and 0 of 814,598 instructions failing to
decode. The coverage figure is a **lower bound** - it counts only bytes proven
reachable, and a further 2.65% of the image is VU microcode rather than MIPS.

Two false-positive traps were worth closing:

* A zero word decodes as a perfectly valid `nop`, so any test that only asks "does
  this decode?" accepts a block of padding as a function. `_looks_like_code` also
  requires real work - at least two non-`nop` instructions and a majority of
  non-padding.
* Seventeen "functions" were sitting inside the read-only data block, decoding
  tables of small integers as instructions on `$zero`, and one pointer array that
  pointed at itself. The return requirement removed all of them.

## `symbols.py` - naming leverage

Three reliable kinds of leaked information:

* **String cross-references.** MIPS materialises a 32-bit address with a
  `lui`/`addiu` pair, or `lui` plus a load offset. Reassembling those recovers
  the constant; when it lands in a string, the call site gains a strong
  human-readable hint. Register tracking resets at any control transfer, so a
  `lui` whose partner sits past a branch is dropped rather than mispaired.
* **RenderWare provenance.** RCS `$Id:` tags name the exact middleware sources
  linked in, identifying which regions are documented-API middleware rather than
  game code.
* **Pointer tables.** Runs of consecutive words pointing at known function
  entries are vtables or jump tables, which reveal C++ class layout. Requiring
  several consecutive valid entries keeps random data from registering.

Everything here generates *hints*. Nothing renames a function without a recorded
reason.

## Overlays - code loaded from the disc

Some games keep most of their code out of the executable, in overlays read from
the disc at run time over memory the executable leaves free (Resident Evil
Outbreak: a 1.4 MB executable, 3.4 MB of overlays, three of them at the same
address). An overlay is decompiled as a game of its own: a directory whose
`game.json` names its base game, its image (unpacked by the game's own tools to
how it lies in memory) and its address (`ps2decomp/overlay.py`). Loading it builds
an executable of the base image with the overlay - and the overlays resident with
it - laid over it, so every tool works on it through `--game` and the interpreter
runs its calls into the executable and the other overlays as they are. The
analysis keeps only the functions in the overlay's `code` ranges; the rest are
the base's, or another overlay's, to decompile.

## Data flow

Paths are relative to the game's directory, as `game.json` names them.

```
disc image
   |  isotool.py
extracted/<executable>
   |  analyze.py   (elf -> analysis -> symbols)
build/<database>.json      functions, regions, strings, xrefs, tables
   |                     \
   |  derive.py           \  progress.py  + config/functions.csv
src/generated/              docs/PROGRESS.md
```

The database is generated once and everything downstream reads it, so the
expensive passes are not repeated. It is not committed - it is reproducible from
a disc image in about five seconds.

```

`docs/GPU.md`:

```md
# The GPU renderer: plan

The port draws with a software GS today (`engine/host/src/gs*.cpp`). It is exact
enough to be the reference, and slow and native-resolution only. The GPU renderer
replaces it for play and for the enhancements (higher resolution, widescreen,
higher frame rates), and is checked against it.

## Decisions

* **Vulkan**, behind the `ps2gpu` library (`engine/gpu`). One backend reaches
  Windows, Linux and Android natively and macOS through MoltenVK. It gives what
  GS emulation needs and portable wrappers do not: blending the fixed-function
  units cannot express (done in the fragment shader with framebuffer fetch or
  feedback loops), the destination alpha test, sampling from what was just
  drawn, and 16- and 24-bit colour and depth.
* **SDL3** for the window, input, events and later audio, on every platform.
  The Win32/GDI window stays as the fallback (`window.cpp`).
* Dependencies come from their releases by CMake FetchContent (Vulkan-Headers,
  volk, SDL3; glslang next), so nothing is installed and nothing of theirs is
  committed.
* The software GS stays: it is the reference the GPU renderer is tested against,
  frame by frame, and the fallback without a GPU.

## Stage one (done): presentation

`ps2gpu::Display` / `CreateVulkanDisplay`: an SDL3 window and a Vulkan swapchain.
Each frame the software GS's picture is copied to a staging buffer and an image
and blitted, 4:3 and letterboxed, to the swapchain image. MAILBOX present mode
where available, so presenting never blocks the emulation thread. Built into the
host with `-DPS2HOST_VULKAN=ON`; `--window` then uses it, and the keyboard is
read through SDL. `ps2gpu_smoke` checks a device, a swapchain and 120 frames.

## Stage two: the GS on the GPU

The GS draws into its 4 MB local memory, which games also read back as textures
(render-to-texture, the frame copies Burnout 3 does every frame from 0x8C0 to
the CT16S display buffer), upload into and copy within. The design follows what
proved itself in PCSX2's hardware renderers, made smaller:

1. **Draw batching.** `Gs::Draw` hands primitives to a renderer interface instead
   of rasterising: vertices in screen space (after XYOFFSET), with the state
   that drew them - PRIM, TEX0/TEX1/CLAMP, ALPHA, TEST, FBA, FRAME, ZBUF,
   SCISSOR, DTHE, COLCLAMP, PABE. A batch runs while the state is unchanged.
2. **Render targets.** A FRAME (FBP, FBW, PSM) is a Vulkan colour image at N x
   the native resolution; a ZBUF a depth image. They are looked up by base
   pointer and format, and created on first use.
3. **Textures.** A TEX0 is looked up in a texture cache keyed by (TBP, TBW, PSM,
   size, CLUT). A miss decodes the region from local memory (the swizzle and the
   CLUT, as `gs_memory.cpp` does) into an RGBA8 image; uploads (`Transfer`) and
   local copies invalidate the pages they touch. A TEX0 that is a render target
   samples the target's image directly - no round trip through local memory.
4. **Shaders.** One vertex shader; one fragment shader specialised (specialisation
   constants) by texture function, alpha test, destination alpha test, fog and
   blending mode. Blending modes the fixed-function blender expresses use it;
   the others read the target in the shader (VK_EXT_rasterization_order_
   attachment_access where present, else a copy). Shaders are GLSL in
   `engine/gpu/shaders`, compiled to SPIR-V at build time by glslang (fetched
   like the others) and embedded.
5. **Read-back.** Where the EE reads local memory (an IMAGE transfer from the
   GS, rare) or a texture covers a target in another format, the target is
   written back to local memory first.
6. **Display.** DISPFB/DISPLAY pick the target that is shown; it is blitted to
   the swapchain as stage one does. PMODE's two circuits and their blending come
   later.

## Testing

* Per frame, both renderers draw the same GIF stream; the GPU frame read back at
  1x is compared with the software frame (`--frames` writes both). Differences
  above a threshold fail; the first differing primitive is found by bisecting
  the stream.
* Burnout 3's frontend - the LOADING screen, menus, the title - are the first
  test scenes, then VU1's 3D.

## Progress

* `GsRenderer` draws triangles - flat or Gouraud, scissored - into R8G8B8A8
  targets keyed by (FBP, FBW, PSM), and reads them back.
* Textures arrive decoded (`UploadTexture`, RGBA with the GS's alpha, under
  a key the host chooses); the fragment shader applies the four texture
  functions with TCC, sampling nearest or bilinear, repeating or clamped.
* The alpha test (ATST, AREF; AFAIL KEEP).
* Blending: `Cv = (A - B) * C + D` maps onto the fixed-function blender as a
  source and destination factor and an operation; C (source alpha or FIX
  over 128) is the fragment's second output by dual-source blending, so the
  alpha written stays the source alpha. One pipeline per ALPHA setting, made
  on first use. Coefficients the blender cannot reach (1 + C, factors over
  1.0, the destination alpha over 128) are approximated.
* The alpha test's AFAIL: FB_ONLY and RGB_ONLY write colour (without depth
  on the GPU yet they are the same), KEEP and ZB_ONLY discard.
* Depth: a D32_SFLOAT buffer per ZBP (and one per target for draws that test
  nothing, since dynamic rendering keeps one attachment layout), holding
  Z / 2^32 - exact for Z24 and Z16, rounded past 24 bits for Z32. ZTST NEVER,
  ALWAYS, GEQUAL, GREATER and ZMSK are dynamic state (Vulkan 1.3), not
  pipelines. `UploadDepth` loads a buffer from local memory's Z; the shadow
  mode does so for each buffer at its first use in a frame.
* AFAIL exactly: a batch whose alpha test can fail draws twice - the passing
  pixels with everything, then the failing ones with what AFAIL keeps
  (FB_ONLY colour, ZB_ONLY depth, RGB_ONLY colour without alpha), the shader
  told which pixels each pass keeps.
* FBMSK as the colour write mask, per byte; fog (FGE, FOGCOL) in the shader.
* The destination alpha test: depth buffers are D32_SFLOAT_S8_UINT; before a
  DATE batch a setup pass (shaders/date.*) samples the target and sets the
  stencil where its alpha bit equals DATM, and the batch draws with a stencil
  EQUAL test.
* Not yet checked against the Vulkan validation layers (not installed on the
  machine this was written on); the results are what the tests check.
* `ps2gpu_tests` checks each of these by reading pixels back.
* **The host drives it**: `--gpu-shadow` (engine/host/src/gpu_bridge.cpp)
  hands every primitive the software GS draws to the renderer as well - its
  FRAME, SCISSOR, TEX0/TEX1/CLAMP, TEST and ALPHA, sprites as two triangles -
  with textures decoded from the software GS's local memory (decoded again
  when their registers change, an upload or local copy happens, or a draw
  goes into their blocks). Each frame, every target drawn into is read back
  and compared with local memory. Burnout 3's frontend, boot to title screen
  and menus, 3,855 frames: 100.0% of pixels agree (within 2 per channel, 8 for
  16-bit formats). The game's frame copy - sprites textured from the frame
  at 0x8C0 into the CT16S display buffer, drawn with ATST NEVER and AFAIL
  FB_ONLY - is what found AFAIL.

## Order of work

1. ~~The renderer interface in the host, with the software GS as one backend~~
   (`Gs::on_draw`, `--gpu-shadow`).
2. ~~Vulkan targets, the batcher and a flat-shaded pipeline~~.
3. ~~Textures~~ (decoded by the host); the texture cache and CLUTs on the GPU
   come with step 6.
4. ~~Blending, alpha and depth tests, fog, FBMSK~~; the destination alpha test
   ~~(DATE, through a stencil pass: the target's alpha bit copied into
   stencil, then the draw tested against it)~~, ~~PABE (a second pass)~~.
5. Upscaling, widescreen (a wider projection where the game's matrices allow).
   With these comes a settings front end: internal resolution and the other
   display options set there are saved (a settings file beside the
   executable) and loaded on every run, command-line options overriding them
   - settings must persist across runs.
6. ~~**The GPU as the renderer**~~ (`--gpu`, engine/host/src/gpu_bridge.cpp):
   the GS model still takes every packet, register and transfer but draws
   nothing (`Gs::rasterize` false); the GPU draws, and its images stand for
   regions of local memory. Each image (a target or a depth buffer) knows the
   blocks it covers - the rows drawn so far, not all the scissor allows - and
   whether the GPU has drawn what memory lacks or memory changed under it.
   * *GS local memory on the GPU*: ps2gpu keeps a copy of the 4 MB, and a
     compute shader (shaders/swizzle.comp) swizzles targets (CT32/24/16/16S)
     and depth buffers (Z32/24/16/16S) into it and out of it, in the GS's
     layout (checked byte for byte against the host's gs::Memory by
     GpuMemorySwizzlesAsTheGs). Per 256-byte block the bridge knows whether
     the CPU's copy, the GPU's, or both are current;
   * *read-backs*: before the GS model reads or writes local memory (an image
     transfer either way, a local copy, a CLUT load, the picture shown) it
     calls `Gs::on_memory` with the blocks; the GPU images over them are
     swizzled into the GPU's copy, and the blocks the CPU lacks come back
     (`MemoryRead`, the one call that waits for the GPU);
   * *uploads*: memory written under an image makes it stale; it reloads
     from the GPU's copy, once the blocks the CPU wrote have gone over
     (`MemoryWrite`), before the GPU next uses it;
   * *aliasing*: an image drawn over another's blocks under another width or
     format (Burnout 3's reflection buffers at 0x16B-0x1A7, the race's blur
     and glow passes in its depth buffer's memory at 0xD2) is swizzled into
     the GPU's copy and the other unswizzled from it - on the GPU, waiting
     for nothing;
   * *submission*: each frame's recorded work is handed to the GPU at the
     frame's end without waiting (`GsRenderer::Kick`, `VulkanGpu::Flush`,
     three command buffers in turn, each with its own fence and vertex
     ring), so the GPU draws one frame while the CPU makes the next; a
     read-back still waits, but for little. The race script waited 32-50 s
     of its ~4 min for the GPU before;
   * *targets as textures*: a TEX0 whose TBP and format match a target's
     samples the target's image;
   * *other textures*: decoded into a cache keyed by TBP/TBW/PSM/TW/TH,
     CLAMP's region modes, TEXA and the CLUT's contents. By the host, from
     the CPU's copy: once memory under one is written its blocks are hashed
     and it is decoded again only if they changed (the car select: 646
     decodes, 239,661 re-sent textures found unchanged). By the GPU, from its
     copy (shaders/decode.comp, every format, CLUT, CSA, TEXA and the region
     modes as the host's TexelAt; GpuDecodesTexturesAsTheGs checks all 14),
     when the GPU holds the blocks newer - the race reads its targets' alpha
     as PSMT8H textures and its depth buffer as PSMZ16, which brought 13 GB
     back to the CPU over 9,550 frames before. The least recently used of
     2,048 released;
   * *FBMSK exactly*: the mask is taken in the target's own format (a 16-bit
     target's five bits a channel are the top of the image's bytes), and a
     channel masked only in part is drawn in two passes with logic ops - AND
     with the bits kept, then OR with the rest of the source - where the
     blend leaves the source as it is (the race writes two bits of each half
     of its frame's 32-bit pixels through a 16-bit view, mask 0x3FFF);
   * *lines and points*: one-pixel bands that cover what the software GS
     plots (the position rounded, both ends);
   * primitives wholly outside the scissor, and ZTST NEVER, are dropped
     before any of this; a draw with ZTST ALWAYS and ZMSK has no depth
     buffer (the race's blur passes leave ZBUF at their own address);
   * *Z over the target's own memory*: with ZTST ALWAYS and Z written, the
     GS writes each pixel's colour and its Z into the same memory, the Z in
     its own layout. The race's glow passes lay their threshold grey down
     that way - as colour over 32 columns and, the Z being the grey, over 32
     more. Such a draw has no depth buffer; its Z is drawn as colour into a
     Z-format view of the memory (and only where the alpha test lets Z be
     written: ATST NEVER with FB_ONLY writes none), and GPU memory reconciles
     the two views.
   The race (race_training.args) was traced this way: a pass-by-pass dump
   (PS2HOST_GPU_DUMP_FRAME) showed the scene right until the glow was added;
   GS memory dumps after frame 9,400 from both renderers (--gs-dump-frame,
   engine/tools/gsmem.py) showed the glow's threshold buffer wrong. Now the
   race's pictures are 98.7-99.9% the same as the software GS's (the rest is
   HUD text blended with factors over 1, which the blender clamps), and its
   glow buffers byte for byte or within 0.5%. The script runs in 8m17s
   against the software GS's 59m36s.
   Checked by running the same scripted input (`--virtual-time`) under both
   renderers and comparing the pictures with `engine/tools/framediff.py`:
   `car_select.args`, 40 pictures from boot to the 3D garage: 35 identical,
   the rest 99.30-99.98% (the globe's light rays, drawn as lines; the
   garage). Keeping GPU and memory in step takes 1.7% of the run.
   The comparison found bugs in the reference too: the software GS drew
   triangles' right and bottom edges (the GS fills top-left) and read
   Z-format textures raw (the GS reads them as their CT formats), and
   `sceCdReadClock` answered wall-clock time under `--virtual-time`, so the
   EA Trax playlist differed between runs.
   Local memory stays the meeting point: the shadow mode's comparison, run on
   a few frames, checks each step.
7. ~~**CLUTs loaded on the GPU.**~~ The submission statistics named what
   waited for the GPU: in the race script all of it was memory read-backs
   (3,134 of them, 25 s of about 2 minutes, around 8 ms each), every one a
   CLUT load - from 0x2CD0, 0x2CD4, 0x2D30 and 0x2D3C - in the crash and
   glow scenes (frames 9,000-10,100), whose CLUTs are images the GPU has
   just drawn: a 192-wide textured blur target over 0x2BC0-0x2D40, sprites
   into the page at 0x2D40 and a 256-point ramp at 0x2D20. (Drawing such
   draws on the CPU as well was tried: only the ramp qualifies, being
   untextured.)
   Now a CLUT load whose blocks the GPU holds newer (`Gs::on_clut_load`) is
   made by the GPU from its own copy of local memory - decode.comp's mode 1,
   CSM1's arrangement, CSA and TEXA as `Gs::LoadClut` - in order with the
   drawing. The bridge keeps the CLUT in rows of 16 entries: which rows the
   GS model holds as loaded, which the GPU's CLUT buffer holds (rows the CPU
   loaded are sent over, `ClutRows`, before a GPU decode reads them). A
   texture reading a row only the GPU has is decoded on the GPU, keyed by the
   row's generation rather than its entries. The race script: 6,138 CLUTs
   loaded on the GPU, 82 read-backs left (0.2 s of waiting, from 29 s),
   "GPU and memory in step" from 29% of the run to 5%; every picture as
   recorded. `GpuDecodesTexturesAsTheGs` checks each palettized format
   through a CLUT loaded on the GPU over a garbage one.

## Pipelines

A pipeline is keyed (`PipelineKey`, `Features` in gs_renderer.cpp) by the
blend and its operands, the write mask and logic op (bits 0-15), and what
the draw may use of gs.frag (bits 16-27, inverted: texturing, a texture
pack's replacement, mipmaps, bilinear filtering, TEXA's expansion, a finer
target, sprite snapping, fog, the alpha test, PABE, logic ops, 16-bit
targets). Those are a specialisation constant: a kind of draw's pipeline
leaves out the rest of the shader - the same results, without the work and
registers of what it never does. On an Intel UHD at 2x the shader was the
GPU's whole time (a trivial shader dropped no frames, the whole one 493 in
the race); specialised, 76-88. Of what is left, the GS's exact bilinear
filter is most, then the alpha test's discards.

In a player's run (a folder for the settings) pipelines come from a cache
kept there (gpu_pipeline_cache.bin) and the keys drawn with are listed
beside it (gpu_pipelines.txt). A worker thread makes them: the listed keys
and the game's own (`SetGpuPipelineHints`) from the start, a new kind of
draw when it first comes - drawn meanwhile with the whole shader's pipeline
for its blend (made at once if there is none). A cold driver takes 0.3-0.7 s
for one; none is made in the middle of a race. Scripted runs keep no cache
and make every pipeline at once, so their pictures test the specialised
shaders. `PS2HOST_PIPELINE_LOG=1` logs each pipeline made and how long it
took; `PS2HOST_GPU_UBERSHADER=1` draws everything with the whole shader.

```

`docs/METHODOLOGY.md`:

```md
# Methodology

## Progress tiers

Every discovered function sits in exactly one tier, recorded in the game's
`config/functions.csv`.

### `undecompiled`

The analysis found the function and knows its address range. Nothing else is
known. Every function starts here.

### `analyzed`

Someone has read the disassembly and written down what the function does - its
argument count, the structure offsets it touches, its role. No source yet. This
captures understanding, which is often the hard part, but it is not code.

### `reconstructed`

C++ source exists and is believed to behave correctly. It has **not** been tested
against the original. Source at this tier is a hypothesis.

### `lifted`

The function has been translated instruction by instruction into C++ over an
explicit register context (`engine/ps2decomp/lift.py`), compiled, and run on the
same test cases against the original. After every case the **whole register
file** and every byte of memory written agreed. That is a stricter comparison than
for derived functions, which compare `$v0` and memory.

Lifted code is emitted in the most readable form that passes. That is structured
(loops and ifs, named locals) where possible, and in the best case with
single-use temporaries folded into their uses. The folded form drops writes to
registers no caller may read, so it is compared at the calling-convention level:
`v0`/`v1`, `$sp`, `$gp`, `$ra`, the callee-saved registers whole, the float
results and callee-saved float registers, and memory. That is the level derived
functions are verified at. Every other form is compared on the whole register
file.

A structured form must pass a second check as well: it is compared with the
function's plain lifted form - verified against the interpreter, and a statement
per instruction - natively, on 2,000 random inputs (`engine/ps2decomp/
equivalence.py`). Both run on the same registers and the same hashed memory; a
call reaches a stub whose effect depends on its target, its place in the
sequence and its arguments; what is compared is what a caller can see. Two
structuring bugs passed the interpreter's random tests because the paths they
broke were never taken, and were found only when a game ran natively; this
check runs a hundred times more cases per function. A form that fails it falls
back to the next, as for a failed verification.

Verdicts are remembered between runs (`engine/ps2decomp/verdicts.py`). A
function's verdict depends only on its own C++ text and the environment it is
tested in - its callees run in the interpreter from the original code - so the
key is the text, the form of comparison, and a fingerprint of the interpreter,
test memory, runtime, verification code, image, analysis and seeds. A verdict
is reused only when all of these are unchanged. A `--no-cache` run recomputes
every verdict and is the check on the two things the key cannot see: the
compiler's version, and the order functions run in within a process.

Lifted source is correct and complete, and enough to run the game on a host, but
it is not readable: it says `c.r[2] = c.r[4] + 5`, not what the function means.
So it is reported as its own tier and never counted as `verified`. A function
that is later derived moves up to `verified`, and its lifted copy is only the
fallback.

### `verified`

The reconstruction has been differential-tested against the original machine code
running in the R5900 interpreter, on a corpus that includes edge cases, and they
agreed. This is the project's bar for done.

**Only `verified` counts as decompiled.** The headline figure in
[PROGRESS.md](../../games/burnout3/docs/PROGRESS.md) reports verified bytes and
nothing else. A second figure, "machine-checked", adds the `lifted` tier: how
much of the program exists as C++ proven to behave like the original, readable or
not.

## Why functional reconstruction, and what it does and does not prove

The original compiler is known - Metrowerks CodeWarrior MIPS 2.4.1.01, named in
the executable's `.comment` section - but it is abandoned proprietary software and
could not be obtained. Without it, byte-matching is impossible: Metrowerks and GCC
differ systematically in register allocation, instruction scheduling and
delay-slot filling, so a GCC attempt would plateau short of a match and never
close.

So the project targets behaviour instead of bytes, and replaces byte-matching with
differential testing:

1. Run the **original machine code** in `engine/ps2decomp/emu.py`, an R5900 interpreter.
2. Run the reconstruction on the same inputs.
3. Compare.

Be precise about the strength of this. A passing differential test shows the two
agree **on the inputs tested**. That is evidence, not proof - a function whose
behaviour depends on an input the corpus never supplies could still differ. The
harness therefore records how many cases ran, puts edge cases ahead of random
ones, and always reports the case count rather than just "passed".

It is a weaker guarantee than byte-matching, and the right response is to say so
rather than to blur the two. What it does give is an objective, automated check
that fails loudly on a regression - which untested source does not.

## Verifying a reconstruction

`engine/ps2decomp/difftest.py` provides the harness for hand-written reconstructions, and
`games/burnout3/tests/test_reconstruction.py` holds those comparisons, so
`python -m unittest discover -s games/burnout3/tests` re-checks every verified function.

`engine/tools/derive.py` does the same job for derived functions, in bulk.

The interpreter covers the integer core, the common loads and stores, 128-bit
`lq`/`sq`, COP1 single precision, and the MMI operations the string routines need -
enough to execute **84.8%** of the 9,163 discovered functions. `$gp` is seeded with
`0x004E8670`, recovered from the startup code, since many functions reach globals
through it.

Anything outside the subset raises `UnsupportedInstruction` rather than being
approximated: an interpreter that quietly guessed would manufacture exactly the
false confidence this exists to remove. The remaining gap is almost entirely VU0
macro mode.

### What is actually compared

Return values are not sufficient. The harness compares **memory effects** too,
because a derivation with the right return value and the wrong store address would
otherwise pass.

Writes are journalled and rolled back rather than restored from a snapshot of a
chosen region. These functions write to globals far outside any such region, and an
earlier version that snapshotted only a scratch area left those changes in place -
which corrupted later cases and made correct derivations look wrong. It could
equally have produced false passes.

Writes into the callee's own stack frame are excluded. The frame is dead the moment
the function returns, and the original spills registers into it constantly while a
derived expression writes none, so counting them would fail every function with a
prologue.

### Automated derivation

Roughly a third of verified functions were not written by hand at all. Small
branch-free and acyclic functions are derived symbolically, differential-tested, and
only then emitted as C++ - see [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md). A derivation that
fails or cannot be executed is dropped rather than emitted with a caveat.

Two honesty rules apply to that output:

* A function counts as `verified` only if the test varied something. A constant or a
  fixed-global read ignores its arguments, so eight argument sets exercise one input
  eight times; those land a tier lower.
* Generated functions keep placeholder `func_XXXXXXXX` names, and recovered types
  placeholder `S_XXXXXXXX_aN` names. The behaviour and the layouts are evidence;
  what a function or type is *for* has not been worked out, and a descriptive name
  invented now would read as a finding later.
* Recovered types are presentation, never trusted for meaning. A memory access is
  shown as a field only when it matches the field exactly, and the compiled form of
  every typed function is run against the original.

### The emitted source is compiled and run too

Verifying a derivation means evaluating its expression tree. What ships is the C++
that tree is rendered to, and for a long time nothing checked that the two agree.
They did not. The renderer printed signed and unsigned comparisons identically, and
C++ promotion rules quietly narrowed 64-bit register arithmetic: `ReadU8(p) << 24`
was an `int` shift, and 419 shifts in the file were undefined behaviour. It all
compiled without a single error.

So `derive.py --emit` now compiles the generated file with MSVC (`/O2`, so the
optimiser gets its chance to exploit undefined behaviour) into a library with a
dispatch table, and runs every function on the same cases its derivation was
verified on, with memory routed back to the interpreter
(`engine/ps2decomp/cppcheck.py`). A function whose compiled form disagrees is dropped
and the file re-emitted. Where no compiler is installed the check says it was
skipped; it never passes by default.

The rules the rendering follows to make this hold:

* Every value is a `u64` register image. Arguments are `u64`, and the `Read*`
  helpers return the loaded value already sign- or zero-extended.
* Operators whose meaning depends on width or signedness carry it explicitly:
  `(s64)` on signed comparisons, `(u64)((s32)x >> n)` for `sra`,
  `(x & 0xFFFFFFFF) >> n` for `srl`, masked variable shift counts, `1ull` for a
  shifted literal.
* Float constants print as exact literals: `FloatBits(-1.0f)`, not `0xBF800000`.
* The reference EE FPU helpers live in `engine/runtime/src/eefpu.cpp`.

### Bugs this process caught

Worth listing, because each argues for the approach. None were visible to
inspection, and several were in the *verifier* rather than the reconstruction:

* `beql`/`bnel` nullify their delay slot when not taken; executing it unconditionally
  clobbered a mask register in the SIMD `strlen`.
* Word and doubleword shifts share one mask in the expression model, and the 5-bit
  one turns a shift of 32 into a shift of zero.
* `lui` was not sign-extended into the 64-bit register.
* The verification harness restored only a scratch region, so writes to globals
  persisted across cases.
* Journalling then exposed that stack-frame writes must be excluded.
* Float registers held as host doubles canonicalised NaN payloads, so a `lwc1`/`swc1`
  copy altered the value. Here the derivation was right and the interpreter wrong.
* An overflowing `mul.s` crashed the interpreter outright, because the EE's FPU is
  not IEEE-754: it has no infinities and saturates to the largest representable
  magnitude. A port must reproduce that rather than "fix" it.
* `simplify` turned an unsigned `sltu` tested against zero into a signed comparison.
  The tests passed only small positive pointers, so both readings agreed.
* Branching void functions were emitted without a `return;` at the end of each
  early path, so it fell through into the later paths' stores. Their multi-store
  paths were also not captured before writing. Compiling and running the output
  found 12 such functions, all of which had passed as trees.
* Word operations (`addu`, `addiu`, `sll`, `sllv`, ...) sign-extend their 32-bit
  result into the 64-bit register; the model kept the full 64-bit value. That is
  invisible unless upper bits are observed, and with only small positive pointers
  as arguments they never were. Passing $t0..$t3 arguments exposed it: an `sllv`
  result reached an `slt`. Word results are now wrapped in a sign extension that
  the simplifier removes wherever only the low 32 bits are used or the value
  provably fits. The first version of that simplification was exponential on the
  shared subtrees of unrolled loops; it is memoised on the (immutable) nodes.
* The first statement emitter for calls captured a value *after* the store that
  changed it, and let a local declared in one branch be used in the other. The
  compiler caught the second; the compiled run would have caught the first.
* Interpreting the original callees made verification slow - decoding every
  instruction from scratch dominated. Decodes are now cached per address, and a
  verification case may run at most 100,000 instructions.
* Declaring float arguments `u32` instead of `u64` made `farg0 & 0x7FFFFFFF` plus
  -127 wrap at 32 bits. The compiled check caught both affected functions.

## The original toolchain, for the record

The executable's `.comment` section names its compiler outright:

```
MW MIPS C Compiler (2.4.1.01)   PlayStation2
```

Metrowerks CodeWarrior MIPS 2.4.1.01 for PlayStation 2. Normally identifying this
is the opening problem of a decompilation; here the build stamped its own identity
into the binary.

It is nonetheless abandoned proprietary software - Metrowerks went to Freescale and
then NXP, and the PS2 product has not been sold in about two decades - which is
why this project verifies behaviour instead of bytes.

If `mwccmips` 2.4.1.01 is ever obtained, byte-matching becomes available as a
*stronger* check on top of the existing one, and `engine/tools/matchdiff.py` is kept for
exactly that: it compares a compiled object against the original image and scores
it both exactly and semantically.

```sh
python engine/tools/matchdiff.py 0x0010BE40 --object games/burnout3/build/syscalls.o --symbol SignalSema
```

The kernel stubs in `games/burnout3/src/kernel/syscalls.cpp` are the natural calibration targets,
being short enough that their source is unambiguous.

## Conventions for reconstructed source

* C++17, since the original is C++ (with RenderWare 3.6 underneath in C).
* Fixed-width types from `engine/runtime/include/ps2rt/types.h`.
* Every reconstructed function carries a comment naming the address it came
  from and its current tier.
* Names that are recovered from evidence (a string, an RTTI entry, a RenderWare
  API signature) are used as-is. Names that are inferred get a comment saying so.
  Never silently invent a name that looks authoritative.
* Structure layouts live in headers, with offsets documented, because they are
  the reusable product of the work.

```

`docs/PORTING.md`:

```md
# From decompilation to a native port

Decompilation produces C++ for each function and proves it equivalent to the
original. A port runs that C++ on a PC. This document describes the layer in
between, the **native host** (`engine/host/`), and how a game becomes an
executable.

## The pieces

```
engine/runtime/   PS2 instruction semantics: FPU, VU0 macro mode, integer edge
                  cases, 128-bit MMI. Shared by verification and the port, so the
                  port runs exactly the semantics every function was verified on.
engine/host/      The PC platform: guest memory, dispatch, the EE kernel, devices.
games/<g>/src/lifted/   The game's translated functions (lift.py --emit).
games/<g>/port/   The game's port: CMakeLists.txt and overrides.cpp
                  (a new game's from engine/templates: port.py init).
```

Translated code reaches its environment only through a few hooks
(`ps2rt/lifted.h`, `ps2rt/generated.h`):

| hook | in verification | in the port |
|---|---|---|
| `ReadU32`, `Write32`, ... | the Python interpreter's memory | `ps2host::Memory`: flat RDRAM, scratchpad, register windows |
| `Call`, `TailCall` | the interpreter runs the original callee | the dispatch table runs the translated callee, or an override |
| `Syscall` | a fixed stub | `kernel.cpp`, the EE kernel's services |
| `Tick` | aborts a runaway loop | the same, with a budget large enough to play |

Because every translated function was verified against the interpreter through
these same hooks, a port is correct exactly as far as its host implements them
faithfully.

## Building and running

```sh
python engine/tools/lift.py --game games/<g> --structure --emit   # translate
python engine/tools/port.py --game games/<g>                      # build and run
python engine/tools/port.py --game games/<g> run -- --trace       # log every call
```

A port is built for processors with AVX2 (`PS2HOST_AVX2`, on by default:
the VU's lanes and the rest in three-operand SIMD, 6% of a race). For those
without it - Intel's Pentium and Celeron of before 2021 (Pentium Silver,
Celeron N, the Pentium Gold of desktops) - `port.py --game games/<g> --sse4
build` builds `<name>-sse4.exe` (SSE4.1, in `build/port/cmake-sse4`, copied
beside the main one); a release ships both. The executable's entry
(`src/cpu_check.cpp`, a library of its own built without AVX) checks the
processor before anything else runs - the runtime's start and static
constructors are AVX2 code too - and on one without AVX2 starts the SSE4
build beside it with the same command line, or says what is needed
(`PS2HOST_TEST_NO_AVX2=1` takes that way on a processor with it). `port.py`
builds with a compiler per 2.5 GB of memory: a file of compiled VU code
takes one 2 GB and more.

Options for finding out why boot stops, passed after `run --`:

| option | what it shows |
|---|---|
| `--trace` | every call, not just the first of each function |
| `--notes` | every host event (DMA, interrupts, SIF, kernel calls), repeats included |
| `--watch ADDR` | each call of the function at ADDR, with its argument registers and `$ra` |
| `--peek ADDR` | 64 bytes of guest memory at ADDR, in the report |
| `--window` | the picture, live, in a window (close it to end the run): SDL3 + Vulkan (`engine/gpu`), or GDI when built without `PS2HOST_VULKAN` or without a Vulkan device |
| `--gs-trace` | every GS image transfer and primitive, with its TEX0 fields |
| `--until-frame N` | stop when frame N is done - with `--virtual-time`, the same point of the game every time |
| `--virtual-time` | the scheduler keeps the clock (each loop slice is 1 ms, waiting skips to the next event): the EE timers, alarms, the IOP and the vblanks follow it, so a scripted run (`--press`) is the same run on any machine under any load; frame-identical across runs |
| `--gpu` | the GPU renderer draws instead of the software GS (`gpu_bridge.cpp`); local memory is kept in step with the GPU's images where the game reads it (transfers, CLUT loads, textures, the picture). Compare its `--frames` with a software run's using `engine/tools/framediff.py` |
| `--gpu-shadow` | the GPU renderer draws every primitive too; each frame its targets are compared with the software GS's (and written beside `--frames` pictures as gpu_/soft_ BMPs) |
| `--gpu-shadow-rtt` | the same, a texture that is a GPU target sampled from the target (render to texture), as the GPU renderer will on its own |
| `--gpu-show` | `--gpu-shadow-rtt`, and the window (`--window`) shows the GPU renderer's picture instead of the software GS's |
| `--gs-trace-frame N` | the same for six frames from frame N (a picture is drawn across several) |
| `--gs-dump-frame N` | GS local memory, all 4 MB, written to `gsmem_N.bin` (in the `--frames` directory) when frame N is done - under `--gpu`, as the GPU has it. `engine/tools/gsmem.py` shows a buffer from a dump, or compares two runs' dumps buffer by buffer |
| `--sample` | a sampling profiler on the EE thread (a thousand samples a second, eight frames deep): at the end, the functions most often running and most often on the stack, by name, and where it was running by source file and line (inlined code by the line inlined: a VU step in vu_core.h, not the block) - the port builds with symbols for it |
| `--gs-inline` | the GS model (and the GPU renderer behind it) on the EE's thread rather than its own (`gs_thread.cpp`): for debugging, and for `--sample` to see the GS's share |
| `--frames-from N` | with `--frames`: only from frame N on (the dump keeps 200 pictures) |
| `--frame-times N` | every N frames, how long they took in wall-clock time, the frame (vertical blank) rate and how many DMA transfers to VIF1 - a game's pictures of 3D, usually one each - went a second (`regress.py --frame-times N` prints them). In real time a game that cannot keep up draws every other blank: Burnout 3's race runs at 58 blanks and 25-30 pictures a second. In real time the line also counts the vertical blanks lost - due while the last was still undelivered, the EE busy through a whole frame - which is what puts a movie's pictures behind its sound |
| `--audio` | the SPU2's mixed output on the sound device, reverb included |
| `--sample-gs` | `--sample` on the GS thread instead (the GS model, the GPU bridge, their submissions) |
| `--sample-vif1` | `--sample` on VIF1's worker (real time: VIF1, VU1 and what they feed the GS) |
| `--vif1-sync` | in real time, VIF1 and VU1 on the EE's thread as under `--virtual-time` (vif1_worker.cpp) |
| `--press BUTTON@FRAME` | hold a pad button for 6 frames from that frame (cross, circle, start, up, ...); `BUTTON@FROM-TO` holds it from one frame to another (`cross@17650-19400`: accelerate through a race); `padN:BUTTON@FRAME` is scripted controller N's (from 1), a device of its own that a game can give player 2 (`SetPortDevices`); repeatable |
| `--key KEY@FRAME` | hold a keyboard key the same way (a letter or digit, enter, escape, space, up, lshift, ... or a virtual key's number, `0x20`): a game's own keys (`SetKeyboardMapper`) in a scripted run; `KEY@FROM-TO` too; repeatable |
| `--real-time-from N` | a `--virtual-time` run goes on in real time from frame N - the clock carrying on, the blanks' timer and VIF1's worker started - so a scripted run gets exactly to what is to be measured, then is measured as played (with the player's settings beside the executable) |
| `--fast-until N[:F]` | in real time, the vertical blanks F times as fast (8 unless said) until frame N, then at their rate: a scripted run's way to the part measured (`PS2HOST_PROFILE_FROM`). Faster than the EE keeps up with, the game falls behind its frame count and the presses miss: Burnout 3's race script holds at 2 |
| `PS2HOST_PROFILE=FILE`, `PS2HOST_PROFILE_FROM=N` | the frame-pacing profiler (`ps2host/timeline.h`): every thread's work and every picture's way to the screen, as a timeline (Chrome's trace format: ui.perfetto.dev), from frame N; at the end a summary - the present intervals' percentiles, the frames dropped or late, and what was busy before each |
| `--mouse FRAME:X,Y[,L\|R\|U\|D]` | the mouse at (X, Y) of the picture (0 to 1 across it) from that frame, its left or right button clicked or the wheel turned up or down then; repeatable. With any, the window's mouse is not read - a scripted run's menus driven by the mouse |
| `--memcard DIR` | a memory card in slot 1, kept as a directory: the game's saves are files there (`ps2host/mc2.h` answers libmc2's handlers; the port binds them). Without it the slot is empty |
| `--setting KEY=VALUE` | a PC setting for this run, not saved (`--setting aspect=16:9`: a scripted run in a wider picture); any number of them |
| `--vu-record FILE`, `--vu-interpret` | record the VU microprograms a run starts, for compiling ahead of time; run them interpreted (see below) |
| `--vu-fast` | compiled VU1 programs leave out the MAC and STATUS flags no instruction of theirs can read ("Fast mode" below): exact but for those flags, ~15% less VU1 time; exact is the default unless the game's port chooses it (`SetVuFastDefault`) |
| `--vu-exact` | VU1's exact flags even where the game's port defaults to fast mode |
| `--audio-wav FILE` | the same output recorded to a WAV file, for checking sound without listening |
| `PS2HOST_AUDIO_LOG=1`, `PS2HOST_AUDIO_MUTE=1`, `PS2HOST_SPU_LOG=1`, `PS2HOST_SPU_NO_REVERB=1` | sound, looked into: every two seconds how the SPU2's samples came (the longest wait between batches) and what the device made of them (ran out, dropped, fewest buffers queued); the device played unheard; once a second the voices sounding, their volumes fixed or sweeping, the main volumes; the reverb left out |
| `--watch-write ADDR` | every store to a guest address, with the function making it and four of its callers |
| `--iop-trace` | every IOP library call the game's own modules make |
| `--timeout S` | the time limit (30 s); `--budget N` makes a run deterministic |

The guest's own debug output (`kputs`) appears as `[guest]` lines.

With `--disc` and no executable, the port boots the one the disc names
(SYSTEM.CNF's `BOOT2`), read from the image. Started with no arguments at
all - from Explorer, or a shortcut - a port built with `ps2_add_port(... GAME
<dir>)` plays: it asks for the player's own disc image the first time (a file
dialog, checked to be the disc game.json's executable comes from), remembers
it in `pc_settings.ini` beside the executable, and runs on the GPU with a
memory card in `memcard/` there, in a window with sound and no time limit.
It is a windowed program, so no console opens beside it: started from a
terminal it writes to that one, and started with no arguments to a log named
after it (`burnout3.log`), which an error message points to.

F1 shows or hides an FPS counter (the pictures shown a second; setting
`fps_counter`, off by default). F9 (or L3 + R3 on a controller) opens the
engine's PC settings panel over
any game (`host/src/pc_menu.cpp`): resolution, aspect ratio, fullscreen,
v-sync, frame pacing and the texture pack, applied at once and saved in
`pc_settings.ini`; the game gets no input while it is open. A port can also
put its settings in the game's own menus (Burnout 3's PC SETTINGS).

The window's title is game.json's `title`. The executable's icon (the
window's and the taskbar's too) is the port's own, `port/icon.ico` - original
art, safe to publish with the port (Burnout 3's from
`port/tools/make_icon_art.py`). A player can give their own build the game's
logo instead: `port/tools/make_icon.py` makes `build/port/icon.ico` from their
disc (the port run to the title screen, the logo's texture taken from GS
memory with `gsmem.py texture`), which `ps2_add_port` takes over the port's
own. Made from the disc, that one is never committed or shared. A `--virtual-time` run
without `--memcard` leaves the player's settings alone and uses the defaults,
so its pictures stay as recorded; `--setting` gives it one of its own.

`port.py` generates `build/port/generated/dispatch.cpp` (every translated
function by address, with names from `config/names.csv`), builds `port/` with
the CMake and Ninja that ship with Visual Studio, and runs the result on the
executable in the game's `extracted/` directory. Nothing from the disc is built
into the port; the user supplies it.

The run ends with a report: why it stopped, the guest call stack at that point,
each thread's state, the kernel services used, and every device register
touched. That report is the port's progress measure, as `progress.py` is the
decompilation's. The first thing in it that the host lacks is the next thing to
implement. A run that goes on longer than `--timeout` seconds (30 by default)
stops at its next loop head and reports where it was. If the host process
itself outlives that by 90 seconds, port.py kills it and says so: that is a
host bug, not the game's.

### Under `--gpu`, for finding what the GPU renderer gets wrong

* `PS2HOST_GPU_LOG=1`: every 100 frames, each GPU image (target, depth buffer,
  view) with how often it was reloaded and why, and what came back to the CPU;
* `PS2HOST_GPU_DUMP_FRAME=N` (and `PS2HOST_GPU_DUMP_DIR`): during frame N, each
  target as drawing leaves it, as a BMP, and a line per pass on stderr with
  FRAME, PRIM, TEX0, ALPHA, TEST and ZBUF - to find the pass where a picture
  goes wrong.

The way in, as for the race (GPU.md): run the same scripted input under both
renderers and compare the pictures (`framediff.py`); find the frame; dump its
passes to find the pass; dump GS memory from both renderers after that frame
to see which buffer differs, and from it which rule of the GS the GPU path
does not keep.

### When a picture is wrong because a translation is

Every lifted form was checked against the original, but only on the inputs
the tests reached. Build the port from the plain lifted form as well (lift.py
without --structure) and compare the scripted run's pictures with the
structured build's: the plain form is mechanical and the better reference.
Where they differ, `engine/tools/bisect_lifted.py` finds the function: it
builds the port from one emission with chosen functions' bodies from the
other, renders the frame, and halves the candidates (the functions the run
calls whose two forms differ) until one is left - twelve builds for the car
select's missing cars (0x0042DAE0, FINDINGS.md). To see how the culprit's
two forms differ, override it in the port with a function that runs both
from the same registers and memory and prints the first difference.

## Speed

Where the time goes: the report's `time:` line (sections, timed with the
timestamp counter) and `--sample` (by function). What it showed, and what was
done about it:

* guest memory: the derived code reaches main RAM inline (`generated.h`,
  `ram_base`); registers, the scratchpad and watched writes go to the port;
* calls: `Dispatch` keeps a direct-mapped cache of address -> function and
  call counter;
* wait loops: under `--virtual-time` a loop spinning until an interrupt spends
  slice after slice; a port names such loops (`ps2host::AddIdleLoop`, the
  loop head) and time goes straight to the next event there. Burnout 3's is
  RenderWare's wait for its DMA buffers to flip (0x001F24E0);
* VU1: each instruction pair is decoded once for its stalls; the integer unit
  runs directly;
* DMA reads plain memory through a pointer.

Further: GS memory addresses come from precomputed pages; the GPU bridge
hands images off by the blocks drawn since their last write-back and writes
back only those rows; batches into the same target share a rendering pass;
COP2's FMAC operations are decoded once (VU and macro mode alike), and
their arithmetic is chosen once an instruction rather than once a lane;
image transfers into GS memory write a row's run of pixels at a time
(the page and its offsets found once a page, not once a pixel).

Further still: DMA hands VIF0, VIF1 and PATH3 a run of words at a time;
the scratchpad channels copy through pointers when no store is watched;
`gs::TheGs()` is inline.

Burnout 3's scripted runs under `--gpu`: the car select from 3m55s to about
43s; the race script from 8m28s to about 3m30s (the software GS: 46
minutes). Each frame's GPU work now runs while the next frame is made
(GPU.md, *submission*). VU1 (an interpreter, with its timing model) and
DMA/VIF are now the largest parts; then the GPU's hand-offs between views of
the same memory. The sampler (`--sample`) shows where: run with it before
choosing what to speed up next. Wall-clock times on a laptop vary by half
again over a day (throttling): compare builds back to back.

Since: an IMAGE packet's quadwords go to the transfer together (Gs::Words);
the FMAC computes four lanes at once in single precision (SSE; the
equivalence with the double-precision model is argued in vu_math.h and
checked by VuLanesAreTheModel); and VU microprograms are compiled ahead of
time (below). Under `--gpu` the car select now takes about 24 s and the
race script about 2 minutes (the software GS: 46 minutes).

Each of these was checked by running the scripted runs and comparing the
pictures with the recorded ones (`engine/tools/regress.py`, runs/README.md).

`--frame-times` showed where the race script really stands: the menus run
at hundreds of frames a second, the race itself (frames 9,300-9,900, the
crash and glow scenes) at 12-22. What `--sample`'s line view found there,
and what was done:

* CLUTs drawn by the GPU loaded on the GPU (GPU.md, step 7): 29 s of the
  script's waiting gone;
* every write to GS memory scanned all 2,048 cached textures for the ones
  it invalidates (3%): textures are now indexed by page;
* each texture checked every GPU image for drawing over it on every
  textured primitive: it keeps the few images that can overlap it;
* timers: three nested timed sections a primitive (73 million in the
  script) cost two clock reads each; the bridge times itself once;
* VU flags landing went through a call nearly every pair (5%): inline;
* UNPACK's data went into a byte buffer a word at a time: whole elements
  are read from the DMA words, and an unmasked element is copied as is
  (DMA and VIF from 23% of the run to 11%);
* compiled VU code: a stall check that can never stall is left out (VF0;
  a field written four or more pairs before in the block; a field the
  block has not written, from its fourth pair: see `needless_wait`), and
  the MAC flags are found for four lanes at once;
